actus.definition: Liturgical action, moral human act (actus humanus, proceeding from deliberate will), or canonical act. — [Classical contrast: Driving of cattle, impulse, motion, performance of a play, or legal right of way.]

potentia.definition: Spiritual power/faculty of the soul (intellect, will, senses); divine omnipotence. — [Classical contrast: Political might, influence, force, or authority.]

essentia.definition: Divine Essence (the one nature of the Father, Son, and Holy Spirit in Trinitarian theology). — [Classical contrast: Rare philosophical neologism coined (according to Seneca and Quintilian) to translate Greek 'ousia'.]

existentia.definition: Actual subsistence or reality of a thing. — [Classical contrast: Post-classical philosophical coinage from ex(s)isto ('to step forth, emerge').]

esse.definition: To be, to exist; divine subsistence. — [Classical contrast: To be, exist, live, stay.]

sum.definition: To be, exist ('Ego sum qui sum', Exod. 3:14 — God as Ipsum Esse Subsistens). — [Classical contrast: To be, exist, live, abide.] • Liturgical usage: "Domine, non sum dignus, ut intres sub tectum meum: sed tantum dic verbo, et sanabitur anima mea." (Lord, I am not worthy that thou shouldst enter under my roof: but only say the word, and my soul shall be healed.)

ens.definition: being; something having esse/existence; (basic concept of St. Thomas Aquinas);

substantia.definition: Consubstantial divine nature (Credo: 'consubstantialem Patri') or the underlying reality of bread and wine converted in the Eucharist. — [Classical contrast: Resources, property, wealth, or material contents.]

accidens.definition: Eucharistic accidents (species of bread and wine remaining after transubstantiation). — [Classical contrast: An unforeseen occurrence, chance event, or misfortune.]

doctrina.definition: Christian teaching, catechesis, authoritative Church doctrine. — [Classical contrast: Instruction, learning, erudition, science.]

scientia.definition: One of the seven gifts of the Holy Spirit (donum scientiae); God's omniscience. — [Classical contrast: Knowledge, skill, acquaintance with a subject.]

sapientia.definition: Divine Wisdom (the Word/Son of God in Wisdom literature and Christology); the highest of the seven gifts of the Holy Spirit. — [Classical contrast: Good sense, prudence, practical wisdom, philosophy.]

gratia.definition: Supernatural grace of God, favor, thanksgiving ('Deo gratias', 'Ave Maria, gratia plena'). — [Classical contrast: Favor, esteem, charm, pleasantness, gratitude; 'gratia' (+ gen.) = for the sake of.]

sacramentum.definition: One of the seven sacraments of the Church (Baptism, Confirmation, Eucharist, Penance, Anointing, Orders, Matrimony); mystery of faith (translating Greek mysterion in the Vulgate). — [Classical contrast: A military oath of allegiance taken by Roman soldiers, or a sum of money deposited by litigants in a civil suit.]

fides.definition: The Catholic Faith, Creed, or supernatural virtue of faith. — [Classical contrast: Trust, reliability, credit, pledge, promise, good faith.]

caritas.definition: Supernatural love of God above all things and of neighbor for God's sake (translating Greek agape in 1 Cor. 13 and 1 John 4: 'Deus caritas est'). — [Classical contrast: Dearness, high price, scarcity of provisions, or natural family affection/esteem.]

ratio.definition: Human reason (as distinct from divine revelation) or formal intelligibility. — [Classical contrast: Reckoning, account, calculation, business affair, plan, method.]

intellectus.definition: Spiritual faculty of understanding; one of the seven gifts of the Holy Spirit (donum intellectus). — [Classical contrast: Perception, comprehension, meaning, sense.]

habitus.definition: Virtuous or vicious disposition of soul; monastic/religious habit. — [Classical contrast: Condition, plight, physical posture, dress, attire.]

forma.definition: Sacramental form (the operative words spoken in administering a sacrament, united to the sacramental matter). — [Classical contrast: Outward shape, figure, physical beauty, mold, stamp.]

materia.definition: Sacramental matter (e.g., water in Baptism, bread and wine in the Eucharist); subject-matter of a treatise or moral act. — [Classical contrast: Timber, building wood, stuff, material, topic.]

obiectum.definition: Object of faith, hope, charity, or moral action. — [Classical contrast: Something thrown in the way, a charge ('obiecta' = objections).]

subiectum.definition: The subject of a science, virtue, or sacrament. — [Classical contrast: That which lies beneath, a subordinate or inferior.]

species.definition: Eucharistic species (the appearances of bread and wine after consecration). — [Classical contrast: Sight, look, outward appearance, pretext, kind, sort.]

quidditas.definition: quiddity, what a thing is, essence of a thing; (answers question quid est res);

simpliciter.definition: Unqualifiedly, absolutely. — [Classical contrast: Simply, plainly, directly, frankly.]

inquantum.definition: Insofar as, to the extent that. — [Classical contrast: To what extent, as far as (written 'in quantum').]

videtur.definition: It seems, it appears. — [Classical contrast: It is seen, it seems good.]

praeterea.definition: Furthermore, besides. — [Classical contrast: Besides, beyond this, hereafter.]

respondeo.definition: To answer, respond liturgically or magisterially. — [Classical contrast: To answer, reply, give a legal opinion.]

beatitudo.definition: Eternal blessedness in heaven; the Evangelical Beatitudes. — [Classical contrast: Good fortune, happiness, felicity (coined by Cicero).]

revelatio.definition: revelation; uncovering, laying bare; Revelation of St. John;

persona.definition: Divine Person (Father, Son, Holy Spirit in the Trinity) or human person. — [Classical contrast: Theatrical mask worn by actors, dramatic role, character, legal party.]

virtus.definition: Moral or theological virtue; miracle; Choir of Angels (Virtutes). — [Classical contrast: Manliness, courage, valor, military excellence, worth.]

causa.definition: First Cause (Causa Prima, God) and secondary causes. — [Classical contrast: Judicial lawsuit, case, pretext, motive, reason.] • Liturgical usage: "Roma locuta, causa finita." (Rome has spoken, the case is closed.)

finis.definition: Ultimate end of man (God); consummation of the world. — [Classical contrast: Boundary, border, limit, territory (pl. fines), termination.]

salus.definition: Eternal salvation of the soul, redemption in Christ ('nostra salus'). — [Classical contrast: Physical health, soundness, bodily safety, welfare, or a greeting.] • Liturgical usage: "Extra Ecclesiam nulla salus." (Outside the Church there is no salvation.)

theologia.definition: Sacred Theology, the science of faith. — [Classical contrast: Mythological or philosophical account of the gods.]

scriptura.definition: Holy Scripture, the written Word of God. — [Classical contrast: Writing, composition, tax on public pastures.]

principium.definition: Origin within the Trinity; first truth/article of faith; opening of Genesis/John ('In principio'). — [Classical contrast: Beginning, commencement, origin, foundation.]

natura.definition: Created nature (perfected by grace); the divine and human natures united in the one Person of Christ. — [Classical contrast: Birth, character, disposition, the physical universe.]

anima.definition: The immortal human soul created immediately by God. — [Classical contrast: Air, breeze, breath of life, vital principle.] • Liturgical usage: "Domine, non sum dignus, ut intres sub tectum meum: sed tantum dic verbo, et sanabitur anima mea." (Lord, I am not worthy that thou shouldst enter under my roof: but only say the word, and my soul shall be healed.)

voluntas.definition: The divine will ('fiat voluntas tua') and human free will. — [Classical contrast: Wish, desire, inclination, good-will, last will/testament.] • Liturgical usage: "Fiat voluntas tua." (Thy will be done.)
